title: Different loves
hook: agape, bhakti, metta, ishq, ren: not one love under many names, but many loves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan: a thread tied on a brother's wrist, a bond of protection. Your line was the thread. Who came to mind? Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

Five words, from five places. Agape. Bhakti. Metta. Ishq. Ren. A greeting card could print them in a circle around a heart and call them all the same thing: love, in five languages. It would be a lovely card. It might also be wrong. Put the five words back where they came from, and they start to pull in different directions. One gives without waiting to be earned. One sings to God. One wishes well to every living being. One burns. One starts at the family table. Today: different loves.

Agape first. It's a Greek word the New Testament uses for love, and in First Corinthians the King James Bible renders it charity: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind.” This is love as a gift, and in the Gospels Jesus stretches it as far as the enemy. Agape points outward, to the neighbor and the stranger. Bhakti is Sanskrit, and in Hindu devotion it means loving God personally, with the whole heart. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the devoted one is dear to him. Bhakti points toward a Beloved with a name and a face. Metta is Pali, from the Buddhist teachings, often put into English as loving-kindness. In the Metta Sutta the image is a mother guarding her only child, and that care is to be stretched toward all beings, without limit. Metta points everywhere at once, and asks nothing back. Ishq is a word Sufi poets use for a love that burns and won't stay polite. Rumi calls love the astrolabe of God's mysteries. Ishq points toward the One, and it aches. Ren is Chinese, from Confucius, often rendered humaneness. Asked about it, Confucius answers: love people. And the Analects say that being a good son and a good brother is its root. Ren starts close, at home, and grows outward through duties. So here's the turn. These aren't five names for one feeling. They differ in who is loved, in what is asked, in where it starts. Metta wishes all beings well; ren begins with your own parents. Bhakti longs for one Beloved; agape reaches the enemy. Each word lives inside its own tradition and means most there. One English word flattens them. Keeping them apart is a way of honoring each.
screen: `AGAPE: THE GIFT, EVEN TO THE ENEMY.` · `BHAKTI: DEVOTION TO A BELOVED.` · `METTA: GOODWILL TO ALL BEINGS.` · `ISHQ AND REN: BURNING, AND HOME.` · then, large: `MANY LOVES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring the five to mind, one at a time. Agape, the gift that reaches the stranger. Bhakti, devotion to the divine. Metta, goodwill to every being. Ishq, the longing that burns. Ren, care that starts at home. Don't choose yet. Let each one pass slowly, like faces in a crowd. Then notice which one stays. Which is closest to how you already love, or how you'd like to. There's no right answer, and it may not be the one you expected. When it's clear, name it silently. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Different loves. Five words from five traditions, each pointing its own way: not one love under many names, but many loves. Today's word.
Your line: many loves. Today, when you love someone, notice which kind it is. The gift, the devotion, the goodwill, the longing, or the care that starts at home. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Each tradition keeps its own word: Christians speak of agape, Hindu devotees express bhakti in song and worship, Buddhists practice metta toward all beings, Sufi poets write of ishq, and Confucian teaching roots ren in family duty.

notes: Claim to check: the Greek behind 'charity' in 1 Corinthians 13:4 is agape (standard, but it is a claim about the Greek text, not stated in the KJV itself).
Ishq described as 'a word Sufi poets use for a love that burns': check with an Islam/Sufi Keeper; no claim about its origin is made.
Bhakti glossed as 'loving God personally, with the whole heart'; metta as 'loving-kindness'; ren as 'humaneness'. Common renderings; Keepers may prefer others.
Analects 1.2 is attributed in the text to Master You (Youzi), not Confucius himself; the script says 'the Analects say', which is accurate. Confirm.
Day 876 (Raksha Bandhan) had no script on disk when this was written; the review follows the index (word Raksha Bandhan, carry 'the thread').
Overlaps in subject with day 819 (Many words for love); this day's angle is that the loves differ in direction and should not be blended.
Auditor: howItsDone reworded ('sing bhakti' was garbled). Content otherwise checked: 1 Cor 13:4 KJV exact; Gita 12.13-14, Metta Sutta, Masnavi 1.110, Analects 12.22 and 1.2 paraphrases accurate.
